title: SYSK Selects: How Lobotomies Work
summary: Rerun Selects episode (originally from 2009) in which Chuck and Josh explain how lobotomies work, tracing the history from early shock therapies and the 1936 Portuguese prefrontal leucotomy by Egas Moniz and Almeida Lima, based on Yale monkey experiments, through Walter Freeman's transorbital "ice pick" lobotomy, notable cases including Rosemary Kennedy and Howard Dully, the decline after thorazine, and the continued use of psychosurgery in the UK. The episode closes with audible.com sponsor reads and a listener mail message about nature and man-made compounds.

segments.title: Rerun intro and framing
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this Saturday Selects rerun of the 2009 lobotomy episode; the hosts banter about the topic and the film One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest.
topics: One Flew Over the Cuckoo's Nest

segments.title: Psychiatric treatment in the 1930s
segments.summary: The hosts describe conditions in asylums of the 1930s, including straitjackets and convulsive treatments: insulin shock therapy, Metrazol, and electroconvulsive therapy, based on the suspected link between epilepsy and mental illness.

segments.title: Moniz's first prefrontal lobotomies
segments.summary: Portuguese doctors Antonio Egas Moniz and Almeida Lima performed the first lobotomies in 1936 by drilling holes in the skull and injecting alcohol, inspired by a 1935 Yale study in which monkeys with prefrontal cortex removed lost emotional outbursts. Moniz was inspired after hearing Fulton present the findings.

segments.title: Frontal lobe function and white matter
segments.summary: The hosts explain the prefrontal cortex's executive functions and how gray and white matter work, and why lobotomy aims to sever white matter connections; Moniz switched from alcohol to a loop-wire instrument through drilled holes.

segments.title: Walter Freeman and the ice pick lobotomy
segments.summary: Walter Freeman, a neurologist, adopted Moniz's approach and developed the faster transorbital ice pick lobotomy, entering through the eye socket with an orbitoclast tapped by a hammer; he operated after electroshock knockout and performed bilateral procedures, sometimes with both hands at once, doing many in a day.

segments.title: Freeman's showmanship, outcomes, and deaths
segments.summary: Lobotomy results varied widely; Freeman called the procedure soul surgery and toured the country performing demonstrations, reportedly in 23 states. Surgeons reacted with revulsion, the USSR banned lobotomies, and in one Iowa visit a patient was killed when a pick slipped while Freeman took a photo.

segments.title: Notable patients: Rosemary Kennedy and Howard Dully
segments.summary: Rosemary Kennedy, sister of John F. Kennedy, was lobotomized at 23 and left with severely impaired speech and function. Howard Dully was lobotomized by Freeman at age twelve at his stepmother's request; decades later he investigated his case and produced the MPR radio piece 'My Lobotomy'.

segments.title: Decline of lobotomy and modern psychosurgery
segments.summary: Lobotomy fell out of use with criticism over misuse on criminals and soldiers and the introduction of thorazine in 1950; Freeman's last lobotomy in 1967 killed a patient and he was banned from surgery. Psychosurgery is still performed in the UK under other names.

segments.title: Audible sponsor read and listener mail
segments.summary: Audible sponsor read promoting free audiobook download, then a listener email from Max arguing that man-made compounds are part of nature. The episode's closing sign-off is included here.
